# Sequence analysis in the browser

This short example uses Biopython, NumPy, pandas, and Matplotlib to analyse a
few synthetic coding sequences. JupyterLite runs Python in your browser: the
notebook and its files remain in browser storage rather than being sent to a
notebook server.

The sequences below are deliberately artificial and are intended only to
demonstrate a reproducible analysis workflow. Run each cell in order.

## Load the packages

The first run may take a little while because Pyodide needs to download the
packages. Later runs can reuse packages cached by your browser.

```{python}
# In the Pyodide kernel, micropip installs packages compiled for WebAssembly.
import micropip

await micropip.install(["biopython", "numpy", "pandas", "matplotlib"])
```

```{python}
from io import StringIO

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from Bio import SeqIO
from Bio.SeqUtils import gc_fraction
from Bio.SeqUtils.ProtParam import ProteinAnalysis
```

## Parse some synthetic sequences

Biopython can read common formats such as FASTA directly. Here the FASTA data
are embedded in the notebook, so this example does not need any external data
files.

```{python}
fasta_text = """>synthetic_alpha illustrative coding sequence
ATGGCTGCTGCTGAAGAATTCGGTCCAAAATGGGACTAA
>synthetic_beta illustrative coding sequence
ATGAAGTTTGCTGGTGGTTCCTACGAACTGAACGCTAACTGA
>synthetic_gamma illustrative coding sequence
ATGCCGATCATCGACAACTTTGCTCGTGAATAG
>synthetic_delta illustrative coding sequence
ATGTCTTCTGAACCGAACGGTTATCTGAAAGCTGGTCCATTTTAA
"""

records = list(SeqIO.parse(StringIO(fasta_text), "fasta"))

for record in records:
    print(f"{record.id}: {len(record.seq)} nucleotides")
```

## Calculate sequence and protein properties

Each DNA sequence is translated up to its terminal stop codon. We then use
Biopython to calculate GC content and two basic properties of the translated
protein.

```{python}
rows = []

for record in records:
    protein = str(record.seq.translate(to_stop=True))
    protein_analysis = ProteinAnalysis(protein)

    rows.append(
        {
            "sequence": record.id,
            "length_nt": len(record.seq),
            "gc_percent": 100 * gc_fraction(record.seq),
            "protein": protein,
            "protein_length": len(protein),
            "molecular_weight_da": protein_analysis.molecular_weight(),
            "aromaticity": protein_analysis.aromaticity(),
        }
    )

results = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("sequence")
results.round(2)
```

## Summarize the measurements with NumPy

```{python}
gc_values = results["gc_percent"].to_numpy()
protein_lengths = results["protein_length"].to_numpy()

summary = pd.Series(
    {
        "mean GC (%)": np.mean(gc_values),
        "GC standard deviation": np.std(gc_values),
        "shortest protein (aa)": np.min(protein_lengths),
        "longest protein (aa)": np.max(protein_lengths),
    },
    name="value",
)
summary.round(2)
```

## Visualize the results

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

results["gc_percent"].plot.bar(
    ax=axes[0], color="#2a9d8f", title="GC content"
)
axes[0].set_ylabel("GC content (%)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("")

results["molecular_weight_da"].plot.bar(
    ax=axes[1], color="#e76f51", title="Translated protein mass"
)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Molecular weight (Da)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("")

for axis in axes:
    axis.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=35)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Try changing the analysis

1. Change one or more codons in `fasta_text`, rerun the cells, and observe
   which measurements and plots change.
2. Add another protein property from `ProteinAnalysis`, such as the predicted
   isoelectric point, to the results table and create a plot for it.
